docs.title: priority-frameworks
docs.text: Pluggable prioritization systems for Go applications. Instead of every consumer hardcoding its own Critical/High/Medium/Low (or P0-P4, or MoSCoW) definition, applications share one canonical framework — and avoid the drift that comes from N near-duplicate copies of the same level order and accepted spellings.

docs.title: Built-in frameworks
docs.text:
Levels are ordered by implementation priority (index 0 = highest) — this ordering drives code actions: items to implement come before items to avoid.

Framework Levels (highest → lowest) Use case Severity Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational Security, incidents, bugs Priority (P#) P0, P1, P2, P3, P4 Engineering work prioritization IETF RFC 2119 MUST, SHOULD, MAY Requirements — what to implement IETF Prohibitions MUST NOT, SHOULD NOT Compliance — constraints to validate MoSCoW Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have Agile, product management General Required, Recommended, Optional, Avoid General-purpose requirement levels

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
• Parse — Framework.Parse(s)/IndexOf(s) accept a level's ID, Name, or any of its Aliases (e.g. "CRITICAL", "Crit", "S1" all resolve to Severity's critical).
  • Emit full or abbreviated — Level.Name is the canonical display form (e.g. "Critical"); Level.Abbreviation is a distinct, opt-in short form (e.g. "CRIT"). Framework.AbbreviationFor(idOrName) returns the abbreviation with a fallback to Name when a level has none (e.g. Priority's "P0" is already minimal). A caller picks whichever fits a given call site — including both, in different places, within the same application.
  • Compare and rank — Framework.Compare(a, b), Highest(), Lowest(), Default(), ActionableLevels().
  • Cross-framework normalization — Normalize, CompareAcross, MapTo translate a level's position onto a common 0-1 scale so two different frameworks (e.g. Severity and MoSCoW) can be compared or converted.
  • Score ranges — ScoreRange.LevelFromScore maps a numeric score (e.g. a CVSS score) to a level; CVSSScoreRange() and PercentageScoreRange() are built in.
  • Level counts — LevelCounts tracks and aggregates counts of items at each level, with Total(), ActionableTotal(), HigherThan(level), and Merge() for combining counts from multiple sources.
  • Custom frameworks — Framework/Level are plain structs; define your own alongside or instead of the built-ins.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go get github.com/grokify/priority-frameworks

See the README for full usage examples, and Releases for version history.

docs.title: Release Notes v0.1.0
docs.text: Initial release of priority-frameworks, a Go library for standardized priority level definitions with cross-framework normalization.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: • Go library for standardized priority level definitions with 5 built-in frameworks and cross-framework normalization

docs.title: Core Types
docs.text:
• Framework and Level types for defining custom priority systems
  • GetLevelByID() and GetLevelByNameOrAlias() lookup functions
  • Support for level aliases (e.g., "Sev1" for "Critical")

docs.title: Built-in Frameworks
docs.text: Framework Levels Use Case Severity Critical, High, Medium, Low, Info Security vulnerabilities, incident response Priority P0, P1, P2, P3, P4 Engineering task prioritization IETF MUST, SHOULD, MAY RFC 2119 requirement levels MoSCoW Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have Product prioritization General High, Medium, Low Simple 3-level prioritization

docs.title: Cross-Framework Normalization
docs.text:
• Normalize() - Convert any level to a 0-100 scale for comparison
  • CompareAcross() - Compare priorities from different frameworks
  • MapTo() - Find equivalent levels between frameworks

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: go get github.com/grokify/priority-frameworks

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import pf "github.com/grokify/priority-frameworks"

// Use built-in frameworks
sev := pf.Severity()
level, _ := sev.GetLevelByID("critical")

// Compare across frameworks
result := pf.CompareAcross(pf.Severity(), "high", pf.Priority(), "P1")
// result == 0 (equivalent priority)

// Map between frameworks
equiv := pf.MapTo(pf.Severity(), "critical", pf.Priority())
// equiv.ID == "P0"

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text:
• Additional frameworks (CVSS, DREAD, STRIDE)
  • JSON/YAML serialization
  • Framework composition and extension

docs.title: Release Notes v0.2.0
docs.text: This release adds score-to-level mapping, level counting, and separates IETF requirements from prohibitions for cleaner prioritization.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Score-to-level mapping with built-in CVSS support
  • Level counting for dashboards and reports
  • IETF RFC 2119 split into requirements and prohibitions frameworks

docs.title: IETF Framework Split
docs.text:
IETF() now returns only requirement levels (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) for prioritization. Prohibition levels have moved to IETFProhibitions().

// Before v0.2.0
ietf := pf.IETF() // 5 levels: MUST, SHOULD, MAY, SHOULD NOT, MUST NOT

// v0.2.0+
ietf := pf.IETF()              // 3 levels: MUST, SHOULD, MAY
prohib := pf.IETFProhibitions() // 2 levels: MUST NOT, SHOULD NOT

Rationale: Requirements and prohibitions serve different purposes: - Requirements (MUST/SHOULD/MAY) are backlog items to prioritize and implement - Prohibitions (MUST NOT/SHOULD NOT) are constraints to validate during compliance checks

docs.title: ScoreRange
docs.text:
Map numeric scores to priority levels:

// CVSS scores to Severity
sr := pf.CVSSScoreRange()
level, _ := sr.LevelFromScore(7.5) // "High"

// CVSS thresholds:
// Critical: 9.0+
// High: 7.0+
// Medium: 4.0+
// Low: 0.1+
// Informational: 0

// Percentage-based
sr := pf.PercentageScoreRange(pf.Severity())
level, _ := sr.LevelFromScore(85.0) // "Critical" (75%+)

docs.title: LevelCounts
docs.text:
Track counts per priority level for dashboards:

counts := pf.NewLevelCounts(pf.Severity())
counts.Add("critical", 2)
counts.Add("high", 5)
counts.Add("medium", 10)

counts.Total()              // 17
counts.ActionableTotal()    // 17 (excludes Informational)
counts.HigherThan("medium") // 7 (Critical + High)
counts.Slice()              // [2, 5, 10, 0, 0]

docs.title: IETFProhibitions Framework
docs.text:
New framework for compliance validation:

prohib := pf.IETFProhibitions()
// Levels: MUST NOT, SHOULD NOT

// Use for constraint checking, not backlog prioritization
for _, constraint := range constraints {
    level := prohib.Parse(constraint.Level)
    if level.ID == "must-not" {
        // Critical compliance violation
    }
}

docs.title: Migration Guide
docs.text:
If you were using IETF's MUST NOT or SHOULD NOT levels:

// Before
ietf := pf.IETF()
level := ietf.Parse("MUST NOT") // worked

// After
prohib := pf.IETFProhibitions()
level := prohib.Parse("MUST NOT") // use prohibitions framework

docs.title: Release Notes v0.3.0
docs.text: This release makes cross-framework normalization more accurate and hardens the score-to-level and level-count APIs against silent failures.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• More accurate cross-framework normalization: levels now spread evenly across the full range
  • Safer ScoreRange lookups with explicit errors for nil frameworks and unknown levels
  • LevelCounts.Valid() to guard against typo'd level IDs

docs.title: Normalization now spans the full range
docs.text:
Normalize(), CompareAcross(), and MapTo() previously computed a level's position as index / total, which biased the top buckets and collapsed the second level of an odd-count framework into Critical. They now use index / (total-1), so the endpoints pin cleanly (index 0 → Critical, last index → Low) and the middle levels distribute evenly.

For the 5-level Severity framework:

// Before v0.3.0                    // v0.3.0+
pf.Normalize(sev, "critical")       // Critical      → Critical (unchanged)
pf.Normalize(sev, "high")           // Critical      → High
pf.Normalize(sev, "medium")         // High          → Medium
pf.Normalize(sev, "low")            // Medium         → Low
pf.Normalize(sev, "informational")  // Low            → Low

Four-level frameworks (MoSCoW, General) already mapped 1:1 and are unaffected. A single-level framework now maps to Critical.

Action: If you persist normalized priorities or compare them across frameworks, re-check the results — odd-count frameworks (Severity, Priority, IETF) will bucket differently.

docs.title: LevelCounts.Valid()
docs.text:
Add() and Increment() create a map entry for any string, so a typo silently inflates Total() while Slice()/ActionableTotal() ignore it. Valid() lets you check first:

counts := pf.NewLevelCounts(pf.Severity())
counts.Valid("critical") // true
counts.Valid("criticl")  // false — catch the typo before Add()

docs.title: Explicit ScoreRange errors
docs.text:
ScoreRange.LevelFromScore() now returns sentinel errors instead of panicking or failing silently:

level, err := sr.LevelFromScore(score)
switch {
case errors.Is(err, pf.ErrNilFramework):   // ScoreRange has no Framework set
case errors.Is(err, pf.ErrUnknownLevel):   // a matched range references a level not in the Framework
case errors.Is(err, pf.ErrScoreOutOfRange): // score outside Min/Max
}

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• ScoreRange.LevelFromScore() no longer panics when Framework is nil, and reports an unrecognized level ID as ErrUnknownLevel rather than returning a nil level with no error.
  • MapTo() returns a pointer to the destination slice element instead of a loop-local copy, matching Parse().

docs.title: Release Notes v0.4.0
docs.text: This release adds a distinct, opt-in short display form to Level, and a few missing shorthand aliases for Severity. No breaking changes.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Level.Abbreviation: a short display form (e.g. "CRIT") alongside the existing Name (e.g. "Critical") — pick whichever fits a given call site, including using both in different places within the same application
  • Framework.AbbreviationFor(idOrName) returns the abbreviation with a fallback to Name when a level has none (e.g. Priority's "P0" is already minimal)
  • Severity gains CRIT/crit, MED/med, and lowercase info as accepted parse aliases

docs.title: Level.Abbreviation
docs.text:
Name already served as the canonical, title-cased display form. Abbreviation adds a short form alongside it, not instead of it:

level := pf.Severity().Parse("critical")
fmt.Println(level.Name)         // "Critical"
fmt.Println(level.Abbreviation) // "CRIT"

// Or via the convenience accessor, which falls back to Name when a level
// has no distinct abbreviation:
fmt.Println(pf.Priority().AbbreviationFor("p0")) // "P0" (Name, no separate Abbreviation)

Abbreviation is always upper-case, as the one canonical value to build from — a caller wanting a different case applies that transform itself rather than the library storing every case variant. It is populated for Severity (CRIT/HIGH/MED/LOW/INFO), MoSCoW (M/S/C/W), and General (REQ/REC/OPT/AVD); left empty for Priority, IETF, and IETF Prohibitions, whose Name is already minimal.

This is a separate concern from Aliases, which only affects parsing (Parse/IndexOf) — adding an alias never changes what Name/Abbreviation emit for a level.

docs.title: New Severity aliases
docs.text: Severity previously had no shorthand alias for Critical ("Crit" only, mixed case) or Medium ("Med" only), and no lowercase "info" for Informational. Now CRIT, crit, MED, med, and info all parse correctly, matching the common CRIT/HIGH/MED/LOW/INFO shorthand convention.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go get github.com/grokify/priority-frameworks@v0.4.0

See CHANGELOG.md for the categorized commit list.
